title: Training health
subtitle: Whether a reinforcement-learning run is evidence or an expensive way to keep a random policy. Every check here is a failure that happened while building this episode.
findings: **The policy has not learned the task.** Sampled rollouts reach 232 m of a 393 m track and finish 38% of laps. Nothing below is a finding about driving; it is a description of an unfinished training run.

**The policy you would deploy is not the policy that was trained.** Sampling its actions gives 232 m and a 38% finish rate; taking its mean action gives 129 m and 0%. The behaviour depends on the exploration noise itself.

**It went outside the tire model.** Worst slip angle 15.2 deg against our 12 deg bound, with 1.0% of steps beyond it. Nothing in the environment stopped it — that constraint exists only inside the optimal-control solver — so the forces out there are arithmetic rather than measurement, and no lap time from this run is comparable with Seasons 1 and 2.

checks.name: policy_is_actually_updating
checks.detail: median approximate KL per update is 0.00302 against a 0.0001 floor. Below the floor the weights are barely moving and the run is a very expensive way to keep a random policy — which is what happened when the value gradient was 150x the policy's and one shared gradient clip scaled both by 0.0067.

checks.name: exploration_is_not_growing
checks.detail: policy entropy went -0.66 -> -0.44 (+0.22). A policy that is learning gets more decisive; rising entropy means the entropy bonus is beating the policy gradient, which on a Gaussian policy it will do indefinitely because entropy is unbounded above.

checks.name: exploration_matches_the_action_scale
checks.detail: holding the 40 m corner needs a normalised steering action of about 0.037; the policy searches with a standard deviation of 0.082, a ratio of 2.2x. Far above and the car saws the wheel off the road before it learns anything; far below and it never finds the behaviour at all.
checks.group: Is the search at the scale of the problem?

checks.name: the_two_action_dimensions_need_different_exploration
checks.detail: Steering rate and throttle have useful scales an order of magnitude apart — 0.037 of authority against the whole [-1, 1] interval — so a single exploration standard deviation cannot serve both. With one value small enough for the steering, the policy never sampled braking at all and sat at full throttle for half a million steps. This run uses [0.082, 0.368].
checks.group: Is the search at the scale of the problem?

checks.name: the_task_is_completable
checks.detail: the car makes 19.3 m/s round this corner at the limit and starts the episode at 15.0 m/s. Starting above the corner speed means the first thing the policy must discover is hard braking, seconds before any consequence, against an immediate reward for going faster — configured that way it never completed a single lap in 250k steps.
checks.group: Is the task possible, and did it get solved?

checks.name: the_off_track_rate_came_down
checks.detail: episodes ending off the road went 1.00 -> 0.08. A rate stuck at 1.00 means every episode is a crash and the policy has never seen the behaviour it is supposed to be reinforcing.
checks.group: Is the task possible, and did it get solved?

checks.name: the_critic_predicts_returns
checks.detail: explained variance over the last fifth of training has a median of +0.57. At zero the critic is no better than predicting the mean, which makes every advantage estimate noise and the policy gradient a random walk.

checks.name: the_deployed_policy_completes_the_task
checks.detail: the mean-action policy — the one you would ship — finishes 0% of laps and covers 129 m. Sampling its actions instead gives 38% and 232 m. **The deployed number is the result.** A run whose sampled policy performs well and whose mean action does not has not produced a driver; it has produced a policy whose competence lives in its own exploration noise, and the sampled figure describes something you cannot ship.
checks.group: Does the policy you would actually deploy work?

checks.name: greedy_and_stochastic_agree
checks.detail: mean-action rollouts reach 129 m and sampled rollouts reach 232 m, a 44% gap. A large gap means the behaviour depends on the exploration noise itself, so the deterministic policy you would ship is a different driver from the one the training curves describe.
checks.group: Does the policy you would actually deploy work?

checks.name: why_the_noise_matters_here
checks.detail: The action-to-force map has a kink at zero — braking authority is 12 kN against 4.5 kN of drive, because brakes really are stronger than engines. A Gaussian policy straddling that kink does not deliver the force of its mean action: E[f(a)] != f(E[a]), and the difference is always toward braking. At a mean throttle of zero the sampled policy delivers about 1.2 kN of net braking that the mean action does not have. **The policy did not learn to brake. It learned a mean action that brakes only when its own noise is added to it.**
checks.group: Does the policy you would actually deploy work?

checks.name: the_policy_stayed_inside_the_tire_model
checks.detail: worst slip angle reached 15.2 deg against our 12 deg bound, with 2.5% of steps beyond it. Every minimum-time solve in Seasons 1 and 2 constrains this; the environment deliberately does not, so the policy is free to operate where the Magic Formula is extrapolating and the forces are arithmetic rather than measurement.
checks.group: Did it stay inside the tire model?

checks.name: the_tire_file_s_own_load_range_was_respected
checks.detail: 1.0% of steps left the tire file's own declared operating range. That bound is the file's, not ours, and outside it the model is not extrapolating from a fit — it has no fit.
checks.group: Did it stay inside the tire model?
